To italicize something means to write, type, or print a word (or a group of words) in a special slanted style, where the letters lean to the right instead of standing straight up.

Here is the simplest way to see it:

  • Normal text looks like this.
  • Italicized text looks like this.

Notice how the letters in the second line are tilted? That is what italicizing does. It makes text look different from the surrounding words on purpose.

Italicizing is never random. It is always done with a reason. Think of it as a tool — you use it to send a signal to the reader. Here are all the main reasons people italicize:

1. To Show Emphasis

When you want a word to stand out and be read with extra stress or importance, you italicize it. It works just like raising your voice on a word when you speak.

I said I wanted coffee, not tea.

Here, italicizing coffee tells the reader: stress this word. It changes the whole feeling of the sentence.

You must submit the form before Friday.

The word must carries urgency. Italicizing it makes that urgency visible on the page.

2. To Write the Titles of Large, Independent Works

When you write the title of a book, a film, a newspaper, a magazine, a play, a television series, an album, or any other large, standalone creative work, you italicize the title.

I just finished reading Pride and Prejudice.

Have you seen Inception?

She reads The New York Times every morning.

Dark Side of the Moon is a legendary album.

The rule here is simple: if the work stands on its own as a complete, independent thing, its title is italicized.

(Note: Short works that exist inside a larger work — like a single song, a poem, or a short story — use quotation marks instead of italics.)

3. To Introduce a New or Technical Word

When a writer introduces a specific term for the first time — especially a technical, scientific, or specialized word — they often italicize it to signal: "pay attention, this is an important new word I am defining right now."

This process is called photosynthesis, which means how plants use sunlight to make food.

The study of the mind is called psychology.

After the word is introduced and defined, it is usually not italicized again.

4. To Write Foreign Words and Phrases

When you use a word or phrase from another language inside an English sentence, you italicize it.

She had a certain je ne sais quoi that made her unforgettable.

The menu listed the dish as pièce de résistance.

This signals to the reader: this word is from a different language. It also makes the sentence easier to read because the foreign word stands out clearly from the English words.

(Exception: Some foreign words have been used in English so long and so often that they are now considered part of the English language — words like "café," "naive," or "résumé." These are usually not italicized anymore.)

5. To Refer to a Word as a Word Itself

Sometimes you are not using a word for its meaning — you are talking about the word itself as an object. In those cases, you italicize it.

The word run has over 600 meanings in English.

What does ephemeral mean?

Avoid using very too often in your writing.

Without the italics, sentences like these can become confusing. Italics make it clear you are discussing the word itself, not using it normally.

6. To Write the Names of Ships, Aircraft, and Spacecraft

The names of specific vehicles like ships, airplanes, and spacecraft are italicized.

The Titanic sank in 1912.

Apollo 11 carried the first humans to the Moon.

7. To Write Scientific Names of Living Things

In science, every living organism has a two-part Latin name (its genus and species). These names are always italicized.

Humans belong to the species Homo sapiens.

The domestic cat is called Felis catus.

In digital writing (on a computer, phone, or tablet): You select the word or words you want, then press a button (usually labeled I in most apps and word processors) or use a keyboard shortcut (Ctrl + I on Windows, or Cmd + I on a Mac). The selected text immediately tilts into italic style.

In handwriting: You simply write the letters in a slightly tilted, slanted style — leaning them to the right. It is not always easy to do cleanly by hand, so in handwritten text, people often underline a word instead to mean "this should be italicized."

In formal written instructions: When someone tells a typesetter or editor that something needs to be in italics, they might underline the word and write "ital" in the margin, because underlining is the traditional handwritten signal for italics.
The Different Forms of the Verb

Since "italicize" is a verb, it changes form depending on how it is used in a sentence:

  • Italicize — base form: Please italicize the title.
  • Italicizes — third person singular: She always italicizes foreign words.
  • Italicized — past tense: He italicized the wrong word.
  • Italicizing — present participle: I am italicizing the book title right now.
A Quick Way to Remember It

Think of italicizing as tilting words to give them a job to do. Every time you see italicized text, ask yourself: why is this tilted? The answer will almost always be one of the reasons above — emphasis, a title, a foreign word, a new term, or a word being discussed as a word.

That is the complete picture of what it means to italicize.
